candidates.tagline: Apple moved Mac Mini's power button to the bottom, said 'nobody uses it,' then needed a macOS patch to skip it entirely.
candidates.story: Apple's Mac Mini M4, released November 2024, relocated the power button to the underside of the device — requiring users to flip or tilt their computer to turn it on; Apple's official defence was that people 'hardly ever use' the power button. After 18 months of mocking (including third-party 3D-printed button extenders going viral), macOS 26.5 added an 'auto-start when plugged in' option specifically so users never need to touch the bottom-mounted button again.
candidates.why_funny: Apple's answer to a badly placed hardware button was to release a software update that makes the button entirely unnecessary — out-engineering their own mistake rather than admitting it.
candidates.alt: Apple Mac Mini M4 compact desktop computer photographed from above and the side, with no visible power button on any accessible surface — because the button is on the bottom

candidates.tagline: Tower Hamlets council installed a padlocked gate in the middle of an active cycle path. The gate is locked. Cyclists cannot open it.
candidates.story: In August 2026, Tower Hamlets council installed a full-width padlocked gate across a marked, heavily-used cycle path in London, with no alternative route and no key for cyclists — prompting widespread ridicule from residents who called it 'car-brained' planning; cyclists arriving at the gate are forced to turn back or lift their bikes around it, while a standard removable bollard would have blocked cars without stopping cyclists at all.
candidates.why_funny: The council chose the most bicycle-hostile possible solution to stop cars from entering a cycle path — accidentally converting an active cycle route into a dead-end.
candidates.alt: A padlocked metal gate installed across the full width of a marked cycle path in Tower Hamlets, London, with cycle lane markings visible on the ground and the locked gate completely blocking access
